corrections.baseline: C++ port of the same density-gradient routine (cpp/lib.cpp, written with Eigen Map/VectorXd/MatrixXd/TensorMap over the caller's arrays; <valarray> is included but unused), called from Julia through @ccall in bench.jl. The published C++ timings were built by the cpp/Makefile of commit 0ebe405 with g++ (Apple clang 11.0.3) -Wall --std=c++11 -O3 -march=native; the current Makefile also passes -fPIC -funroll-loops, which were added later.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: C++: g++ is Apple clang 11.0.3 (clang-1103.0.32.62). The published timings (commit 0ebe405, 2021-05-17) used -Wall --std=c++11 -O3 -march=native with vendored Eigen headers; -fPIC (2021-05-19) and -funroll-loops (2021-05-22) were added afterwards without re-timing (the author reports no effect). Julia 1.6.0 (LLVM 11.0.1) was run with -O3 -C skylake --check-bounds=no and JULIA_NUM_THREADS=1. The published Julia timings (commit 5e99401, 2021-05-22) timed ChemInt.jl's jl_density_gradient!, not the in-repo julia/eval_gradrho.jl; that file (StaticArrays, @views, @inbounds) was added in commit 302ee4b and was never timed in the README. Fortran: gfortran 10.2.0 -O3 -march=native -funroll-loops -fPIC; Rust: rustc 1.52.1 with target-cpu=native, LTO and 1 codegen unit.
corrections.caveats: This is a cross-run comparison. The C++ timings (19.656/45.770/123.619 us) date from commit 0ebe405 (2021-05-17) and the Julia timings (20.021/41.737/112.843 us) from commit 5e99401 (2021-05-22), and the two were never re-measured together. The Julia numbers were taken with the external ChemInt.jl package's jl_density_gradient!, whose repo github.com/zyth0s/ChemInt.jl returns 404. The in-repo Julia port, julia/eval_gradrho.jl (StaticArrays version, commit 302ee4b), was never timed. The C++ timings predate the -fPIC and -funroll-loops flags in the current Makefile. The C++ port uses Eigen dynamic matrices, not std::valarray. The margin is small: about 9% on C2H4 and imidazol, while C++ is about 2% faster on CH4. Fortran is 1.68x faster than Julia on imidazol (derived from page data), and Rust also beats Julia there. The author writes that differences between compiled languages should be due to implementation differences, and titled the commit that produced these Julia numbers 'Julia is == Rust & C++'. Each case is one BenchmarkTools minimum (10 evaluations per sample) on a macOS laptop. The repo has had no commits since 2021-05-29 and has 5 stars.
corrections.why_faster: No mechanism is shown. Both ports run the same loop nest and both heap-allocate per-call scratch arrays: Julia's zeros() and C++'s Eigen VectorXd/MatrixXd. The author attributes differences between compiled languages to implementation differences, not to the language, and the ~9% gap rests on a cross-run comparison.

However, .github/workflows/benchmarks.yml runs C (job bench-c) and LuaJIT (job bench-lua) as separate jobs on separate ubuntu-latest runner VMs with no CPU model recorded, so the 1.28x is a cross-machine comparison (cross-run precedent: D). The C side is also built at -O2, not -O3.

corrections.hardware: GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest runners (x86_64). Each language runs in its own workflow job (bench-c, bench-lua, ...) and so on its own runner VM, and the results are only collected afterwards. No CPU model is stated, and the C and LuaJIT runs may have used different CPUs. Single-thread environment variables are set.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: C: gcc 13.3.0 -std=c99 -O2 (the Makefile copies benchmarks/c2.csv, built from bin/perf2, into benchmarks/c.csv; the workflow passes no extra CFLAGS), linked with OpenBLAS. LuaJIT 2.1.1703358377 from Ubuntu's apt luajit package, run as 'luajit lua/perf.lua'.
corrections.caveats: Cross-machine comparison: C and LuaJIT run in separate GitHub Actions jobs (bench-c, bench-lua) on separate shared runner VMs with no CPU model recorded. The C side is built at -O2, not -O3. The work is dominated by formatting libraries, not compiled user code. C calls glibc fprintf(f, "%ld %ld\n", ...), which parses the format string in vfprintf on every line. LuaJIT's trace recorder (recff_format in src/lj_ffrecord.c) specialises string.format to the constant '%d %d\n' and turns each plain %d into an integer-to-string conversion (lj_strfmt_wint in src/lj_strfmt.c), and f:write then calls fwrite. So the gap is LuaJIT's runtime formatter against glibc printf, not a code-generation win (inference from the sources; the suite states no mechanism). Rust is faster still at 4.17 ms (0.52x). This is the only one of 8 benchmarks that goes LuaJIT's way. It is slower than C on the other seven: recursion_fibonacci 5.20x, userfunc_mandelbrot 2.54x, matrix_statistics 2.29x, recursion_quicksort 2.24x, parse_integers 1.21x, matrix_multiply 1.14x, iteration_pi_sum 1.07x. Times are best-of-15 minimums in milliseconds. The suite is maintained by the Julia project and is first-party for Julia but third-party for LuaJIT.
corrections.why_faster: Runtime library and JIT specialisation, not code generation for user code. LuaJIT compiles string.format with a guard on the constant format string, so the format is parsed once at trace-record time, and each plain %d becomes its own integer-to-decimal routine (lj_strfmt_wint) appended to a buffer, written with fwrite. The C side runs glibc's generic vfprintf, which re-parses '%ld %ld\n' for each of the 100,000 lines. This is inferred from src/lj_ffrecord.c recff_format and src/lj_strfmt.c in LuaJIT v2.1; the suite states no mechanism.
